name: Ant (Ant Silver JavaScript engine)
baseline: Node.js (V8); the same table also lists Bun (JavaScriptCore) and Deno (V8)
workload: Cold start: import Hono, register two routes, print ready and exit (examples/npm/hono/bench-coldstart.js), measured with hyperfine, 10 warmup runs and 100 timed runs.
claimed_speedup: Mean 3.9 ms for Ant vs Node 29.4 ms (Node 7.50x slower), Bun 8.8 ms (2.26x slower), Deno 18.6 ms (4.74x slower); README also lists a 9 MB binary vs about 140 MB for Node.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the timed build. Source builds default to meson buildtype=release, optimization=3, gnu23 and gnu++23 (meson.build); release binaries are built with LLVM/Clang (BUILDING.md).
hardware: Apple M5 Pro, 64 GB RAM, 18 cores, macOS 27.0; Ant 14.1.aa53d9d1.0, Node 26.5.1, Bun 1.4.0, Deno 2.9.5 (README environment table).
tradeoffs: Independent engine (Ant Silver) with a JIT built on a fork of MIR, not a wrapper around V8, JSC or SpiderMonkey. Targets the WinterTC Minimum Common API rather than full Node.js compatibility. test262 pass rate is about 66% (35590/53578 at revision 2026-09-13), compat-table 100%.
caveats: Measures only the cold start of a tiny script, which favours a small runtime with little initialization work; it says nothing about peak throughput. The third-party js-engine-benchmark (V8 v7 suite, github.com/ahaoboy/js-engine-benchmark, ubuntu row) scores Ant 2186 vs Node 40333, about 18x lower than V8-based Node (derived from page data), but 1.8x QuickJS 1217 (derived). Node, Bun and Deno are prebuilt release binaries with far more features and startup work. Single machine; the README does not say which Ant build was timed.
found_via: GitHub: ahaoboy/js-engine-benchmark README table (ant row, C), then the raw README of theMackabu/ant

name: Mobius
workload: Eight checksum-verified micro-benchmarks (integer arithmetic, fib(30), dense array ops, string-key table ops, string ops, nested loops, object create and destroy, mixed workload), median of five runs, in milliseconds.
claimed_speedup: README total 373.9 ms vs Lua 443.3 ms (0.84x of Lua's time) and CPython 1424.8 ms (0.26x, about 3.8x faster, derived from page data). Mobius is slower than Lua on fib(30) (1.23x), dense arrays (1.03x) and string-key tables (1.22x), and slower than CPython on string ops (1.69x), object create/destroy (1.14x) and the mixed workload (1.15x).
compiler_and_flags: buildy.yaml release configuration: C++17, -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -flto on Linux; which build produced the README table is not stated.
tradeoffs: Embeddable C/C++ scripting language with fibers, channels and worker threads, optional type locking, and a large built-in library (JSON, HTTP, SQLite, WebSockets). Version 0.1.0; no TLS yet. Integer division and modulo follow C semantics (truncating), unlike Lua and Python, per benchmarks/run_benchmarks.py.
caveats: The README table disagrees with the committed benchmarks/benchmark_summary_latest.json on the main branch (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bholcomb/mobius/main/benchmarks/benchmark_summary_latest.json): there Mobius totals 0.547 s vs Lua 0.420 s (Mobius about 1.3x slower than Lua, derived from page data) and CPython 1.419 s (Mobius about 2.6x faster). So the CPython win reproduces in the repo data but the Lua win does not. Hardware, Lua build and CPython version are not stated. Micro-benchmarks only; brand-new project with 3 stars.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'faster than Lua / faster than CPython bytecode virtual machine C++ benchmark' surfaced bholcomb/mobius; README Performance section and benchmarks/ directory opened

name: pqR (a pretty quick implementation of R)
baseline: GNU R (derived from R-2.15.0; the NEWS compares with R-3.4.0)
workload: Assorted R operations named in the release notes, for example paste and paste0 on character vectors and replacing parts of vectors or lists; the README states that the modifications substantially improve the speed of R.
claimed_speedup: NEWS: paste and paste0 are 'about two to six times faster than in R-3.4.0, and are usually faster than the stri_paste function from the stringi package'; replacing part of a vector or list with [ ], [[ ]] and $ is 'often faster', by up to a factor of two or more for scalar index and value.
tradeoffs: Source-compatible modification of R-2.15.0 (with some modules from R-2.15.1 and later), so it lags current R releases and package compatibility; adds some language extensions such as preliminary automatic differentiation. Includes the R packages and Fortran/C sources of the R distribution.
caveats: Claims are release-note statements without a benchmark script, hardware or compiler flags in the files read; the speedup baseline R-3.4.0 dates from 2017, not current GNU R. The project web page pqR-project.org was not opened. Last release 2020-07-23, so a modern GNU R (byte-compiled, 4.x) may have closed some gaps.
found_via: GitHub: radfordneal repository list (pqR, 'a pretty quick version of R'), then raw README and NEWS

name: Lightstorm
baseline: mruby bytecode VM (inferred: the README chart labels the reference bar only 'Baseline', and Lightstorm compiles mruby bytecode)
workload: aobench ray-tracing benchmark (openbenchmarking aobench) compiled ahead of time to C through LLVM versus the interpreted baseline.
claimed_speedup: README: 'The compiled version (rightmost) decreases total execution time by nearly ~30%'. Reading the aobench.png bar chart: time about 78% of baseline for Compiled and about 71% for Compiled + escape + CSE; cache misses about 47% and 43% of baseline (values read off the chart).
compiler_and_flags: Generated C is built with -g -flto -O3 (LIGHTSTORM_CFLAGS in CMakeLists.txt); toolchain LLVM 19, CMake 3.28 or newer, ninja.
tradeoffs: Minimalistic ahead-of-time Ruby compiler (simplified Firestorm that targets C, built on mruby); it is not a full CRuby/MRI replacement and compiles only what the project supports.
caveats: One benchmark (aobench) and the numbers exist only in a PNG chart; the baseline is not named in the README (inferred mruby, not CRuby MRI or YJIT); no hardware, compiler version or run count; last commit December 2024.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/mruby page (DragonRuby/lightstorm, C++), then raw README and aobench.png

name: Cinder (Meta's CPython fork with method JIT)
baseline: CPython 3.8 (cpython38_gcc.json in the PERF file); the 3.10-branch README describes Cinder as a fork of CPython 3.10
workload: pyperformance 1.0.1 suite (about 60 benchmarks), cpython38_gcc.json vs cinder_jit_noframe_gcc.json, run 2021-04-21.
claimed_speedup: README: the JIT 'can achieve 1.5-4x speed improvements on many Python performance benchmarks'. PERF file: richards 104 ms to 29.4 ms (3.53x faster), deltablue 11.1 ms to 4.09 ms (2.72x), raytrace 2.00x, float 1.99x, scimark_sor 1.99x, logging_silent 2.82x; but 2to3 4.62x slower, nqueens 1.56x slower, python_startup 18.00x slower.
compiler_and_flags: gcc (named in the result file names); flags not stated.
hardware: Linux 5.2.9 x86_64 with 48 logical CPUs; CPU model not stated (PERF file header).
stars_or_usage: 3.8k stars; used in production at Meta and Instagram
tradeoffs: Explicitly 'not supported' for outside users (README: Is this supported? Short answer: no); JIT is enabled with -X jit and usually driven by a jit-list file; Static Python needs type annotations; the 3.10 branch is Linux x64 only; the default branch now tracks CPython 3.14 and the JIT ships as the cinderx extension.
caveats: Numbers are from 2021 and compare a Cinder build against CPython 3.8, not like-for-like versions with the later README; 'noframe' JIT mode; several benchmarks regress badly (python_startup 18x slower, 2to3 4.62x slower), so the headline 1.5-4x covers only the benchmarks that JIT well; CPU model unstated and compiler flags unstated; first-party measurement.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'Python runtime in C++ faster than CPython Skybison Cinder Pyjion', then facebookincubator/cinder README (cinder/3.10 branch) and its PERF file

name: Escargot
baseline: QuickJS (Bellard 2026-06-04); the dashboard also lists V8 d8 and V8 d8 --jitless 15.5.35.14, both of which are faster
workload: SunSpider (26 scripts), Octane and Web Tooling Benchmark in native engine shells on one aarch64 CPU of a Linux AWS host, measured 2026-10-04; memory is fixed-work RSS from three fresh processes.
claimed_speedup: vs QuickJS: SunSpider 823.2 ms vs 981.6 ms (1.19x faster), Octane 2198 vs 1689 (1.30x), Web Tooling 1.07 vs 0.89 runs/s (1.20x) (ratios derived from page data). Memory (average RSS): Octane 85.7 MiB vs QuickJS 161.4, V8 137.9; Web Tooling 171.6 vs QuickJS 375.9, V8 331.0. Against V8 --jitless it is slower: SunSpider 694.6 ms, Octane 2300, Web Tooling 2.02 runs/s.
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release with ESCARGOT_DEPLOY=ON, ESCARGOT_THREADING=ON, ESCARGOT_TCO=ON, ESCARGOT_ENABLE_SHELL=ON (tools/monthly-engine-benchmark.py); compiler version not recorded.
hardware: Self-hosted arm64 runner, Linux 6.8.0 AWS aarch64, benchmark pinned to CPU 0; CPU model not named (BogoMIPS 243.75).
stars_or_usage: 364 stars; used in shipping Samsung products
tradeoffs: Bytecode interpreter with no JIT or executable memory; targets ES2026 with ICU-backed Intl and Temporal; designed for memory-constrained devices (Tizen, Android, RTOS); LGPL-2.1 with Apache-2.0, BSD, MIT and MPL-2.0 components.
caveats: Faster than QuickJS only; slower than V8 and even V8 --jitless on all three throughput suites. First-party monthly CI dashboard whose builds of QuickJS (release tarball) and V8 (Homebrew bottle) use other toolchains; SunSpider is 5 repetitions on one core; CPU model not named. SunSpider memory is higher than QuickJS (14.2 vs 5.3 MiB average). ARM32 results were not read.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/javascript-engine?l=c++ page, then the README performance section and gh-pages latest.json/latest.svg through raw.githubusercontent.com

name: lo (just-js)
workload: v8-v7 suite (Richards, DeltaBlue, Crypto, RayTrace, EarleyBoyer, RegExp, Splay, NavierStokes) run daily in CI by a third party on ubuntu, macOS arm64 and windows runners.
claimed_speedup: Score 43804 vs Node 40333 on ubuntu (1.09x), 52785 vs 37405 on macOS arm64 (1.41x), 40191 vs 35121 on windows (1.14x) (ratios derived from page data); also above Bun and Deno on all three platforms.
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu, macos-arm64 and windows runners; CPU models not stated.
tradeoffs: V8-based runtime with custom C++ bindings and assembly builtins, x64 and arm64; minimal Node.js API compatibility; builds link system libssl and zlib plus a custom libcurl.
caveats: lo's own README makes no performance claim; the evidence is only the third-party daily table (lo version 0.0.33.pre). Because lo embeds V8, the gap to Node reflects V8 version, flags and runtime setup rather than a new engine, and plain V8 d8 scores higher still on ubuntu (48107). The v8-v7 suite is old and hardware is whatever the CI runner provides.
found_via: GitHub: ahaoboy/js-engine-benchmark README results tables (lo row), found via WebSearch on JavaScript engine benchmarks

name: JavaScriptCore (WebKit)
workload: v8-v7 suite (Richards, DeltaBlue, Crypto, RayTrace, EarleyBoyer, RegExp, Splay, NavierStokes) run daily in CI by a third party; JavaScriptCore vs V8 on ubuntu, macOS arm64 and windows.
claimed_speedup: macOS arm64 score 67664 vs V8 64220 (1.05x, derived from page data); RegExp 31307 vs 16440, Richards 52925 vs 47206; V8 is ahead on DeltaBlue (142147 vs 76961) and EarleyBoyer (123391 vs 104765). On ubuntu V8 wins (48107 vs 45928) and on windows V8 wins (46932 vs 41169).
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu, macos-arm64 and windows runners; CPU models not stated.
tradeoffs: Part of WebKit; engines are prebuilt by the suite's author, so the build configuration is not the project's own.
caveats: Known project: this is extra evidence only. JSC beats V8 only on macOS arm64, by about 5%, and loses on ubuntu and windows; the v8-v7 suite is old and the runner hardware is unnamed. License and last-commit date were not read this session.
found_via: GitHub: ahaoboy/js-engine-benchmark README results tables, found via WebSearch on JavaScript engine benchmarks
